title: The 1500-Byte Packet That Did Not Arrive in 12 Microseconds
featured_title: THE 1500-BYTE PACKET THAT DID NOT ARRIVE IN 12 MICROSECONDS

presentation.challenge: Serialization took only 12 microseconds. The fiber path added another 500 microseconds.

practice.primary_question: Why are packet transmission delay and propagation delay different quantities?
practice.typical_exam_trap: Using packet size divided by link rate as the entire end-to-end link delay and ignoring physical propagation time.

case_dna.target_misconception: On a fast link, packet size divided by bit rate is the total time for a packet to reach the far end.
case_dna.why_plausible: L/R is a standard networking formula, but it measures serialization onto the link rather than travel time through the medium.
case_dna.contradicting_evidence: A 1500-byte packet on a 1 Gbit/s link takes 12 microseconds to transmit, while 100 km of fiber at 2×10^8 m/s adds 500 microseconds of propagation.
case_dna.corrected_model: Transmission delay is L/R. Propagation delay is distance/propagation speed. A basic one-link latency estimate includes both.

problem_statement: A 1500-byte packet crosses a 100 km fiber link operating at 1 Gbit/s. A network note predicts about 12 microseconds of link delay using packet size divided by bit rate. The first bit cannot reach the far end that quickly. Calculate transmission and propagation delay separately and estimate their sum.

gates.label: Incident
gates.heading: The serialization math was right. The latency conclusion was not.
gates.prompt: Which delay depends on distance rather than packet size?

options.label: Transmission delay is L/R; propagation delay is d/v; both contribute
Transmission and propagation delay are the same quantity
options.reason: One depends on packet length and link rate; the other depends on path length and signal speed.

options.label: A 1 Gbit/s link makes propagation delay negligible by definition
options.reason: Link bit rate does not determine signal propagation speed through the medium.

gates.label: Predict
gates.heading: Predict the propagation delay
gates.prompt: How long (microseconds) does a signal take to traverse 100 km at 2×10^8 m/s?

gates.label: Experiment
gates.heading: Time the link
gates.result: The simple transmission-plus-propagation estimate is about 512 µs.

gates.label: Gap
gates.heading: Prove the two delay components
gates.prompt: Calculate total delay = (1500×8 / 10^9) + (100,000 / 2×10^8). Enter the result in microseconds.
gates.success: Transmission = 12 µs; propagation = 500 µs; total ≈ 512 µs.
gates.hint: Convert bytes to bits and kilometers to meters.

gates.label: Evidence
gates.heading: The two formulas isolate different causes

cards.text: 1500 bytes = 12,000 bits, so L/R = 12 µs at 1 Gbit/s.
Ignoring processing and queueing, the simple one-link total is about 512 µs.

gates.label: Redline
gates.heading: Correct the latency note
report: C2. The link rate is 1 Gbit/s.
C3. Therefore the far-end link delay is only 12 µs.

claims.label: C3
claims.reason: It treats transmission delay as the whole link latency and omits propagation.

evidence_choices.label: Propagation alone is 500 µs across the 100 km fiber
evidence_choices.reason: This shows why a 12 µs total cannot be correct.

correction.template: Transmission plus propagation delay is about {total} µs before queueing and processing.

gates.label: Design Fix
gates.heading: Reduce serialization delay without changing the path length
gates.constraint: Keep packet size and 100 km fiber distance unchanged.

options.label: Increase link rate from 1 Gbit/s to 10 Gbit/s
options.reason: Transmission delay falls from 12 µs to 1.2 µs, though the 500 µs propagation delay remains.

options.label: Send the same packet with a different IP address
options.reason: Address choice does not reduce L/R or physical propagation time.

options.label: Remove propagation delay from the calculation
options.reason: That changes the model, not the physical link.

gates.label: Transfer
gates.heading: Apply the transmission-delay rule
gates.prompt: A 1000-byte packet is sent on a 100 Mbit/s link. What is the transmission delay?

options.label: 10 µs
options.reason: This does not convert bytes to bits correctly.

options.label: 800 µs
options.reason: This is ten times too large.

gates.explanation: Transmission delay depends on packet length in bits divided by link bit rate.

gates.label: Sign Off
gates.heading: Sign off the latency model
gates.confirmation: I confirm that network-link latency can include distinct transmission and propagation components.

items.label: What failed
items.value: The predicted arrival time used serialization delay as total link delay.

items.label: What was missed
items.value: Physical propagation across 100 km of fiber.

items.label: Corrected model
items.value: Compute L/R and d/v separately, then combine the applicable delay components.

seo.seo_title: Transmission vs Propagation Delay: 1500 Bytes Over 100 km | FE E-039
seo.meta_description: Solve FE Case E-039: a 1500-byte packet takes 12 µs to transmit at 1 Gbit/s but 500 µs to propagate across 100 km of fiber.
seo.excerpt: A fast bit rate reduces serialization time, but it does not remove the physical travel time across the link.
seo.direct_answer: Transmission delay is packet length divided by link rate, L/R. Propagation delay is distance divided by signal speed, d/v. For 1500 bytes at 1 Gbit/s, transmission is 12 µs; for 100 km fiber at 2×10^8 m/s, propagation is 500 µs.
